findings.statement: point reads over a drained store are at least 1.25x faster with inline runs
findings.detail: inline 7888498 reads/s (127 ns) against blocks 6124451 (163 ns): inline vs blocks: greater 1.291x (p=0.0051, rel_iqr 1.9%/0.9%). An inline read touches the hash slot and the record; a block-backed one goes on to the block table row and the block, two more misses at a million keys

findings.statement: the store on disk is within 1.05x either way
findings.detail: 3.3 MB with inline runs against 3.3 with blocks (0.999x); device bytes 9.2 against 9.2 MB. Values move from blocks into records; nothing is duplicated, and both arms drop the flat index's half-again record slack a segment never uses

findings.statement: the ordered scan is no slower with inline runs
findings.detail: inline 58023320 entries/s against blocks 74383178: inline vs blocks: NO DIFFERENCE (ratio 0.757, p=0.0656) -- within noise, not a result. The scan walks records in key order and an inline run is where the walk already is; a block-backed one resolves a block per run of keys

findings.statement: the dictionary count over inline records costs at most 2x the block-backed form's per key
findings.detail: 38.32 ns/key through scan_counts over inline records against 20.13 over block-backed ones (1.903x). Wider records mean more bytes per key under the walk; this is the price, registered rather than discovered

findings.statement: ingest-to-routed with inline runs is no slower than with block-backed runs
findings.detail: inline 512843 ops/s against blocks 506199: inline vs blocks: NO DIFFERENCE (ratio 1.013, p=0.6761) -- within noise, not a result. Seal 0.012s against 0.012s, merge 0.011s against 0.011s. The bytes are the same either way; with the records-first layout they stream during the pass instead of being built in memory and written at finish, which is what made the first layout 0.807x

notes: two arms interleaved in one process, fresh store per rep, one option apart: inline_bytes 0 (every run in a block) against 256 (a run up to 256 bytes lives in its index record and a read of it touches no block). The EXT.23 shape: 1M keys, 100-byte values, durable batches, the drain inside the load window, then point reads, one ordered scan of everything, and a dictionary count (scan_counts) over every partition -- all over the drained, routed store
